items.stem: What is the main purpose of accounting?
options: To provide financial information that helps users make economic decisions
To prepare documents for the bank
To calculate the tax a business must pay
items.answer: To provide financial information that helps users make economic decisions
items.markingKey: To provide financial information that helps users make economic decisions. Accounting records, summarises and communicates financial information for decision making [1]

items.stem: Which user of financial statements is most interested in the short-term liquidity of a business?
items.answer: A trade supplier
items.markingKey: A trade supplier. Suppliers want to know if they will be paid within the credit period [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between book-keeping and accounting.
items.answer: Book-keeping is the detailed recording of transactions in books of prime entry and ledgers; accounting uses those records to prepare, analyse and interpret financial statements for users.
items.markingKey: Book-keeping: recording of transactions [1]; accounting: summarising/interpreting/communicating information [1] [2]

items.stem: Diego owns Baobab Furnishings. Copies of the annual financial statements are given to the tax authorities and a trade supplier. State the information the tax authorities would be most interested in and explain why.
items.answer: The profit for the year, to assess the tax payable.
items.markingKey: Information: the profit for the year [1]; reason: to assess the tax payable [1] [2]

items.stem: Ethan owns Fjord Fisheries. Copies of the annual financial statements are given to a trade supplier and the tax authorities. (a) State the information a trade supplier would be most interested in and explain why. (b) Explain why the tax authorities would use the financial statements.
items.answer: (a) Liquidity (working capital) and the record of paying on time, to decide whether to give credit and how much. (b) The tax authorities would use them to look at the profit for the year, to assess the tax payable.
items.markingKey: (a) Information: liquidity (working capital) and the record of paying on time [1]; reason: to decide whether to give credit and how much [1] [2] (b) Information: the profit for the year [1]; reason: to assess the tax payable [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a trade supplier and a bank may be interested in different parts of a business's financial statements.
items.answer: A supplier is concerned with short-term liquidity (current assets against current liabilities) because credit is short term; a bank lending long term looks at profitability, gearing and security over several years.
items.markingKey: Supplier – short-term liquidity [1]; bank – ability to repay over longer period/security [1]; reason linked to time horizon [1] [3]

items.stem: The owner of Harbour Electrics has been asked to send copies of the business's latest income statement and statement of financial position to a prospective partner and to a trade supplier. (a) State the information a prospective partner would be most interested in and explain why. (b) Explain why a prospective partner and a trade supplier might reach different conclusions from the same financial statements.
items.answer: (a) Profitability, ROCE and the value of net assets, to decide whether to invest capital in the business. (b) Their decisions differ: one focuses on profitability, ROCE and the value of net assets, the other on liquidity (working capital) and the record of paying on time, over different time horizons.
items.markingKey: (a) Information: profitability, ROCE and the value of net assets [1]; reason: to decide whether to invest capital in the business [1] [2] (b) Different decisions/interests [1]; different time horizon or information focus [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the accounting equation?
items.answer: Assets = Capital + Liabilities
items.markingKey: Assets = Capital + Liabilities. Resources (assets) are financed by the owner (capital) and outsiders (liabilities) [1]

items.stem: Explain why the accounting equation always balances.
items.answer: Every asset of the business has been financed either by the owner (capital) or by outsiders (liabilities); each transaction has two equal effects, so the equation stays in balance.
items.markingKey: Assets financed by capital or liabilities [1]; dual effect of every transaction [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why profit increases the capital of a sole trader.
items.answer: Profit belongs to the owner; it increases net assets of the business, so the amount the business owes the owner (capital) increases by the same amount.
items.markingKey: Profit belongs to owner [1]; net assets and capital rise equally [1] [2]

items.stem: Tundra Outdoor, owned by Arjun, started the month with total assets of $57,500 and total liabilities of $6,500. The following then took place: (i) bought inventory on credit for $3,400 (ii) sold goods costing $2,100 for $7,700 cash. Calculate the owner's capital at the start of the month.

Savanna Tours, owned by Tomás, started the month with total assets of $47,500 and total liabilities of $9,500. The following then took place: (i) received $4,400 from a credit customer (ii) bought inventory on credit for $8,400 (iii) bought office equipment for $6,100, paying by bank transfer. (a) Calculate the owner's capital at the start of the month. (b) State the effect of transaction (i) on the accounting equation.
items.answer: (a) $38,000 (b) One asset (bank) increases and another (receivables) decreases.
items.markingKey: (a) $47,500 − $9,500 = $38,000 [1] (b) one asset (bank) increases and another (receivables) decreases [2]

items.stem: On 1 January Tomás had business assets of $98,000 and liabilities of $31,000. During January the business: (i) paid a trade payable $4,900 by bank transfer (ii) bought office equipment for $2,500, paying by bank transfer (iii) repaid $3,700 of the bank loan (iv) paid an extra $1,700 of capital into the business bank account. (a) Calculate the owner's capital at the start of the month. (b) State the effect of transaction (iii) on the accounting equation.
items.answer: (a) $67,000 (b) Assets (bank) and liabilities (loan) both decrease.
items.markingKey: (a) $98,000 − $31,000 = $67,000 [1] (b) assets (bank) and liabilities (loan) both decrease [2]

items.stem: On 1 January Kenji had business assets of $110,000 and liabilities of $20,000. During January the business: (i) withdrew $8,400 from the business bank account for personal use (ii) sold goods costing $2,400 for $5,000 cash (iii) repaid $7,400 of the bank loan (iv) paid rent of $7,300 from the bank account. (a) Calculate the owner's capital at the start of the month. (b) Explain why the capital figure in the accounting equation does not tell Kenji how much the business could be sold for.
items.answer: (a) $90,000 (b) Capital is a book value based on historical cost; the sale price depends on market values of assets and goodwill.
items.markingKey: (a) $110,000 − $20,000 = $90,000 [1] (b) Book value at historical cost [1]; market value/goodwill differs [1] [2]

items.stem: Coral Bay Foods, owned by Elena, started the month with total assets of $38,000 and total liabilities of $14,500. The following then took place: (i) received a bank loan of $5,100 (ii) sold goods costing $600 for $6,400 cash (iii) paid a trade payable $5,700 by bank transfer (iv) bought office equipment for $2,300, paying by bank transfer (v) received $500 from a credit customer. (a) Calculate the owner's capital at the start of the month. (b) Calculate total assets, total liabilities and capital at the end of the month.
items.answer: (a) $23,500 (b) Assets $43,200; liabilities $13,900; capital $29,300

items.stem: Distinguish between a current liability and a non-current liability, giving an example of each.
items.answer: A current liability is due for payment within 12 months, e.g. trade payables or an overdraft; a non-current liability is due after more than 12 months, e.g. a five-year bank loan.
items.markingKey: Current: due within 12 months + example [1]; non-current: due after 12 months + example [1] [2]

items.stem: Pampas Leather, owned by Kenji, started the month with total assets of $102,000 and total liabilities of $38,000. The following then took place: (i) bought inventory on credit for $3,600 (ii) received a bank loan of $3,000 (iii) paid rent of $800 from the bank account. A trainee accountant calculated the closing capital as $64,800. Explain why this is wrong and determine the correct closing capital.
items.answer: The decrease in capital from drawings/expenses was added to capital instead of being deducted. Correct closing capital: $63,200.
items.markingKey: Error explained: the decrease in capital from drawings/expenses was added to capital instead of being deducted [1]; working: $107,800 − $44,600 [1]; correct closing capital: $63,200 [1] [3]

items.stem: On 1 January Arjun had business assets of $79,500 and liabilities of $12,000. During January the business: (i) bought office equipment for $6,100, paying by bank transfer (ii) received a bank loan of $5,700. Calculate the owner's capital at the start of the month.

On 1 January Kenji had business assets of $134,500 and liabilities of $15,500. During January the business: (i) withdrew $4,600 from the business bank account for personal use (ii) paid a trade payable $1,500 by bank transfer (iii) bought office equipment for $1,800, paying by bank transfer (iv) received $6,100 from a credit customer (v) sold goods costing $400 for $500 cash. (a) Calculate the owner's capital at the start of the month. (b) Calculate total assets, total liabilities and capital at the end of the month.
items.answer: (a) $119,000 (b) Assets $128,500; liabilities $14,000; capital $114,500

items.stem: Complete the statement: An increase in an asset is recorded as a …
options: credit entry in the asset account
credit entry in the bank account only
debit entry in the asset account
debit entry in the capital account
items.answer: debit entry in the asset account
items.markingKey: debit entry in the asset account. Assets and expenses increase on the debit side [1]

items.stem: Explain the principle of double entry.
items.answer: Every transaction has two aspects of equal value; one account is debited and another is credited with the same amount, so total debits always equal total credits.
items.markingKey: Two aspects/dual effect [1]; equal debit and credit entries [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why drawings are debited to a drawings account rather than to the capital account directly.
items.answer: A separate drawings account collects all withdrawals during the year so their total is visible; it is transferred to capital at the year end, keeping the capital account uncluttered.
items.markingKey: Collects withdrawals in one place/shows total [1]; transferred to capital at year end [1] [2]

items.stem: The following transactions took place at Fjord Fisheries during March: (i) received commission of $2,450 by bank transfer (ii) sold goods on credit to Tariq, $1,400. For each transaction, state the account to be debited and the account to be credited.
items.answer: (i) Dr Bank, Cr Commission received; (ii) Dr Tariq, Cr Sales
items.markingKey: (i) Dr Bank, Cr Commission received [1]; (ii) Dr Tariq, Cr Sales [1] [2]

items.stem: Transactions of Mekong Rice Mills for the week ending 14 June: (i) paid wages of $4,100 by bank transfer (ii) withdrew $1,950 cash from the bank for office use (iii) returned goods costing $2,550 to Diego. For each transaction, state the account to be debited and the account to be credited.
items.answer: (i) Dr Wages, Cr Bank; (ii) Dr Cash, Cr Bank; (iii) Dr Diego, Cr Purchases returns
items.markingKey: (i) Dr Wages, Cr Bank [1]; (ii) Dr Cash, Cr Bank [1]; (iii) Dr Diego, Cr Purchases returns [1] [3]

items.stem: Arjun owns Coral Bay Foods. In one week the business returned goods costing $650 to Mei; the owner paid $2,650 of personal savings into the business bank account; bought goods for resale on credit from Mei, $4,350 and Ines returned goods sold for $1,100. For each transaction, state the account to be debited and the account to be credited.
items.answer: (i) Dr Mei, Cr Purchases returns; (ii) Dr Bank, Cr Capital; (iii) Dr Purchases, Cr Mei; (iv) Dr Sales returns, Cr Ines
items.markingKey: (i) Dr Mei, Cr Purchases returns [1]; (ii) Dr Bank, Cr Capital [1]; (iii) Dr Purchases, Cr Mei [1]; (iv) Dr Sales returns, Cr Ines [1] [4]

items.stem: Ravi owns Sahara Solar. In one week the business paid rent of $2,000 in cash; returned goods costing $1,450 to Sofia; sold goods on credit to Sipho, $1,550 and received commission of $3,450 by bank transfer. (a) For each transaction, state the account to be debited and the account to be credited. (b) Explain why a trial balance that agrees does not prove that every transaction has been posted to the correct account.
items.answer: (a) (i) Dr Rent, Cr Cash; (ii) Dr Sofia, Cr Purchases returns; (iii) Dr Sipho, Cr Sales; (iv) Dr Bank, Cr Commission received (b) Errors such as commission, principle, omission and complete reversal keep debits equal to credits.
items.markingKey: (a) (i) Dr Rent, Cr Cash [1]; (ii) Dr Sofia, Cr Purchases returns [1]; (iii) Dr Sipho, Cr Sales [1]; (iv) Dr Bank, Cr Commission received [1] [4] (b) Equal debits and credits still possible [1]; any named example of error not revealed [1] [2]

items.stem: Transactions of Jade Ceramics for the week ending 14 June: (i) returned goods costing $4,450 to Diego (ii) sold goods on credit to Mei, $2,700 (iii) bought office furniture for $5,100, paying by bank transfer (iv) paid rent of $4,950 in cash (v) bought a delivery van for $18,800 on credit from Summit Motors. (a) For each transaction, state the account to be debited and the account to be credited. (b) Explain why transaction (iv) is recorded in this way.
items.answer: (a) (i) Dr Diego, Cr Purchases returns; (ii) Dr Mei, Cr Sales; (iii) Dr Office furniture, Cr Bank; (iv) Dr Rent, Cr Cash; (v) Dr Motor vehicles, Cr Summit Motors (b) Expense increases – debit; cash (asset) decreases – credit.
items.markingKey: (a) (i) Dr Diego, Cr Purchases returns [1]; (ii) Dr Mei, Cr Sales [1]; (iii) Dr Office furniture, Cr Bank [1]; (iv) Dr Rent, Cr Cash [1]; (v) Dr Motor vehicles, Cr Summit Motors [1] [5] (b) expense increases – debit; cash (asset) decreases – credit [2]

items.stem: Explain why expenses and assets are both recorded on the debit side.
items.answer: Both represent uses of the business's resources; an expense reduces capital (which has a credit balance), so it is a debit, and an asset is a resource held, also a debit.
items.markingKey: Expenses reduce capital – debit [1]; assets are resources owned – debit [1] [2]

items.stem: The following transactions took place at Volcano Spices during March: (i) sold goods on credit to Leila, $3,600 (ii) paid rent of $3,150 in cash. For each transaction, state the account to be debited and the account to be credited.
items.answer: (i) Dr Leila, Cr Sales; (ii) Dr Rent, Cr Cash
items.markingKey: (i) Dr Leila, Cr Sales [1]; (ii) Dr Rent, Cr Cash [1] [2]

items.stem: The following transactions took place at Sahara Solar during March: (i) received commission of $4,400 by bank transfer (ii) sold goods on credit to Omar, $2,800 (iii) the owner took goods costing $5,700 for personal use. For each transaction, state the account to be debited and the account to be credited.
items.answer: (i) Dr Bank, Cr Commission received; (ii) Dr Omar, Cr Sales; (iii) Dr Drawings, Cr Purchases
items.markingKey: (i) Dr Bank, Cr Commission received [1]; (ii) Dr Omar, Cr Sales [1]; (iii) Dr Drawings, Cr Purchases [1] [3]

(a) For each transaction, state the account to be debited and the account to be credited. (b) Explain why a trial balance that agrees does not prove that every transaction has been posted to the correct account.
items.answer: (a) (i) Dr Sofia, Cr Sales; (ii) Dr Drawings, Cr Purchases; (iii) Dr Leila, Cr Purchases returns; (iv) Dr Rent, Cr Cash; (v) Dr Bank, Cr Sofia (b) Errors such as commission, principle, omission and complete reversal keep debits equal to credits.
items.markingKey: (a) (i) Dr Sofia, Cr Sales [1]; (ii) Dr Drawings, Cr Purchases [1]; (iii) Dr Leila, Cr Purchases returns [1]; (iv) Dr Rent, Cr Cash [1]; (v) Dr Bank, Cr Sofia [1] [5] (b) Equal debits and credits still possible [1]; any named example of error not revealed [1] [2]

items.stem: In which ledger is the personal account of a credit customer kept?
items.answer: Sales ledger
items.markingKey: Sales ledger. Trade receivables' accounts are in the sales (receivables) ledger [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between a cash transaction and a credit transaction.
items.answer: In a cash transaction payment is made at the time of the sale or purchase; in a credit transaction payment is made later, so a receivable or payable is created.
items.markingKey: Cash – immediate payment [1]; credit – payment later, creates receivable/payable [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a business keeps a separate ledger account for each credit customer.
items.answer: So that the amount owed by each customer is known, statements can be sent and overdue debts chased.
items.markingKey: Know amount owed by each customer [1]; credit control/statements [1] [2]

items.stem: Orchid Pharmacy sells goods on credit. The following relate to the account of Ana in the sales ledger for May: (i) 1 May balance owed by Ana $4,750 (ii) 6 May credit sale to Ana $4,500 (iii) 11 May Ana returned goods $220 (iv) 20 May Ana paid $2,790 by bank transfer and was allowed $55 cash discount. Prepare the account of Ana for May, balancing it at 31 May.
items.answer: Debit side: balance b/d $4,750, sales $4,500; credit side: sales returns $220, bank $2,790, discount allowed $55, balance c/d $6,185; balance b/d 1 June $6,185 (debit)
items.markingKey: Debit entries (b/d, sales) [1]; credit entries (returns, bank, discount) [1]; balance c/d $6,185 [1]; b/d on debit side [1] [4]

items.stem: Pampas Leather sells goods on credit. The following relate to the account of Nadia in the sales ledger for May: (i) 1 May balance owed by Nadia $3,390 (ii) 6 May credit sale to Nadia $3,730 (iii) 11 May Nadia returned goods $50 (iv) 20 May Nadia paid $2,360 by bank transfer and was allowed $50 cash discount (v) 28 May credit sale to Nadia $2,220. Prepare the account of Nadia for May, balancing it at 31 May.
items.answer: Debit side: balance b/d $3,390, sales $3,730, sales $2,220; credit side: sales returns $50, bank $2,360, discount allowed $50, balance c/d $6,880; balance b/d 1 June $6,880 (debit)
items.markingKey: Debit entries (b/d, sales) [1]; credit entries (returns, bank, discount) [1]; balance c/d $6,880 [1]; b/d on debit side [1] [4]

items.stem: Information about the customer Mei in the books of Atlas Engineering: (i) 1 May balance owed by Mei $4,420 (ii) 6 May credit sale to Mei $1,240 (iii) 11 May Mei returned goods $250 (iv) 20 May Mei paid $3,280 by bank transfer and was allowed $90 cash discount (v) 28 May credit sale to Mei $2,880. (a) Prepare the account of Mei for May, balancing it at 31 May. (b) Name the account in the general ledger to which the discount is debited.
items.answer: (a) Debit side: balance b/d $4,420, sales $1,240, sales $2,880; credit side: sales returns $250, bank $3,280, discount allowed $90, balance c/d $4,920; balance b/d 1 June $4,920 (debit) (b) Discounts allowed account (an expense).
items.markingKey: (a) Debit entries (b/d, sales) [1]; credit entries (returns, bank, discount) [1]; balance c/d $4,920 [1]; b/d on debit side [1] [4] (b) Discounts allowed [1]

items.stem: Complete the statement: A cash sale is recorded by …
options: debiting cash and crediting the customer
debiting the customer and crediting sales
items.answer: debiting cash and crediting sales
items.markingKey: debiting cash and crediting sales. No receivable arises for a cash sale [1]

items.stem: Explain what a debit balance on a supplier's account would mean.
items.answer: The business has paid the supplier more than it owes (e.g. overpayment or returns after payment), so the supplier owes the business – it is an asset.
items.markingKey: Supplier owes the business/overpayment [1]; treated as an asset/receivable [1] [2]

items.stem: Baobab Furnishings sells goods on credit. items.answer: Debit side: balance b/d $1,870, sales $1,040, sales $1,350; credit side: sales returns $310, bank $1,360, discount allowed $110, balance c/d $2,480; balance b/d 1 June $2,480 (debit)
items.markingKey: Debit entries (b/d, sales) [1]; credit entries (returns, bank, discount) [1]; balance c/d $2,480 [1]; b/d on debit side [1] [4]

items.stem: Which activity is book-keeping rather than accounting?
options: Recording sales invoices in the sales journal
Advising the owner on whether to expand
Preparing a budget for next year
items.answer: Recording sales invoices in the sales journal
items.markingKey: Recording sales invoices in the sales journal. Book-keeping is the routine recording of transactions; accounting summarises, interprets and communicates [1]

items.stem: The owner of Atlas Engineering has been asked to send copies of the business's latest income statement and statement of financial position to the owner and to a prospective partner. State the information the owner would be most interested in and explain why.
items.answer: The profit for the year and the value of the business, to judge whether the business is worth continuing and how much can be withdrawn as drawings.
items.markingKey: Information: the profit for the year and the value of the business [1]; reason: to judge whether the business is worth continuing and how much can be withdrawn as drawings [1] [2]

items.stem: The owner of Tundra Outdoor has been asked to send copies of the business's latest income statement and statement of financial position to the bank manager and to a major customer. (a) State the information the bank manager would be most interested in and explain why. (b) Discuss whether the published profit figure is the most useful information for the bank manager.
items.answer: (a) Liquidity and the ability to repay loans with interest, to decide whether to lend or extend an overdraft. (b) Profit shows performance, but the bank manager may need cash flow, liquidity or security information too; profit can be affected by accounting policies.
items.markingKey: (a) Information: liquidity and the ability to repay loans with interest [1]; reason: to decide whether to lend or extend an overdraft [1] [2] (b) Profit useful – performance/ability to pay [1]; other information needed (liquidity, cash, security) [1]; judgement [1] [3]

items.stem: A business has assets of $85,000 and liabilities of $23,000. What is the capital?

items.answer: Liabilities were added to assets instead of being deducted (capital = assets − liabilities). Correct closing capital: $95,500.

items.markingKey: Error explained: the entries were reversed (complete reversal); liability to supplier decreases – debit; purchases returns (reduction of expense) – credit [1]; working: correct accounts named on each side [1]; correct double entry: debit Daniel, credit Purchases returns [1] [3]

items.answer: (i) Dr Bank, Cr Capital; (ii) Dr Office furniture, Cr Bank

items.stem: Atlas Engineering sells goods on credit. The following relate to the account of Sofia in the sales ledger for May: (i) 1 May balance owed by Sofia $4,710 (ii) 6 May credit sale to Sofia $1,130 (iii) 11 May Sofia returned goods $250 (iv) 20 May Sofia paid $420 by bank transfer and was allowed $50 cash discount (v) 28 May credit sale to Sofia $1,250. A junior clerk calculated the balance owed by Sofia at 31 May as $6,870. Explain why this is wrong and determine the correct closing balance.
items.answer: Sales returns were added to the account instead of being credited (deducted). Correct closing balance: $6,370.
items.markingKey: Error explained: sales returns were added to the account instead of being credited (deducted) [1]; working: $7,090 − $250 − $420 − $50 [1]; correct closing balance: $6,370 [1] [3]

items.stem: Information about the customer Priya in the books of Cedar Hardware: (i) 1 May balance owed by Priya $4,890 (ii) 6 May credit sale to Priya $910 (iii) 11 May Priya returned goods $90 (iv) 20 May Priya paid $2,160 by bank transfer and was allowed $20 cash discount. Prepare the account of Priya for May, balancing it at 31 May.
items.answer: Debit side: balance b/d $4,890, sales $910; credit side: sales returns $90, bank $2,160, discount allowed $20, balance c/d $3,530; balance b/d 1 June $3,530 (debit)
items.markingKey: Debit entries (b/d, sales) [1]; credit entries (returns, bank, discount) [1]; balance c/d $3,530 [1]; b/d on debit side [1] [4]

items.stem: Which is an internal user of the financial statements of a sole trader?
items.answer: The owner
items.markingKey: The owner. The owner/manager is inside the business [1]

items.stem: Monsoon Garments is a sole-trader business. Its financial statements are read by several groups, including the bank manager and a prospective partner. State the information the bank manager would be most interested in and explain why.
items.answer: Liquidity and the ability to repay loans with interest, to decide whether to lend or extend an overdraft.
items.markingKey: Information: liquidity and the ability to repay loans with interest [1]; reason: to decide whether to lend or extend an overdraft [1] [2]

items.stem: Aisha owns Andes Supplies. Copies of the annual financial statements are given to a major customer and a prospective partner. (a) State the information a major customer would be most interested in and explain why. (b) Discuss whether the published profit figure is the most useful information for a major customer.
items.answer: (a) The long-term survival of the business, to be sure of continued supplies and after-sales service. (b) Profit shows performance, but a major customer may need cash flow, liquidity or security information too; profit can be affected by accounting policies.
items.markingKey: (a) Information: the long-term survival of the business [1]; reason: to be sure of continued supplies and after-sales service [1] [2] (b) Profit useful – performance/ability to pay [1]; other information needed (liquidity, cash, security) [1]; judgement [1] [3]

items.stem: Which transaction increases both assets and liabilities?
options: Receiving cash from a credit customer
items.answer: Buying inventory on credit
items.markingKey: Buying inventory on credit. Inventory (asset) and trade payables (liability) both rise [1]

items.stem: On 1 January Lucas had business assets of $131,000 and liabilities of $21,500. During January the business: (i) bought office equipment for $1,700, paying by bank transfer (ii) paid a trade payable $2,500 by bank transfer. A junior clerk calculated the closing capital as $147,500. Identify the error and state the correct closing capital.
items.answer: Liabilities were added to assets instead of being deducted (capital = assets − liabilities). Correct closing capital: $109,500.
items.markingKey: Error: liabilities were added to assets instead of being deducted (capital = assets − liabilities) [1]; correct closing capital: $109,500 [1] [2]

items.stem: On 1 January Mohammed had business assets of $70,000 and liabilities of $32,000. During January the business: (i) bought office equipment for $1,300, paying by bank transfer (ii) received a bank loan of $7,900. Calculate the owner's capital at the start of the month.

On 1 January Tomás had business assets of $54,500 and liabilities of $9,000. During January the business: (i) paid a trade payable $1,600 by bank transfer (ii) paid an extra $7,500 of capital into the business bank account (iii) paid rent of $7,500 from the bank account. (a) Calculate the owner's capital at the start of the month. (b) State the effect of transaction (iii) on the accounting equation.
items.answer: (a) $45,500 (b) Assets fall and capital falls because the expense reduces profit.
items.markingKey: (a) $54,500 − $9,000 = $45,500 [1] (b) assets fall and capital falls because the expense reduces profit [2]

items.stem: Coral Bay Foods, owned by Priya, started the month with total assets of $36,500 and total liabilities of $11,500. The following then took place: (i) sold goods costing $5,700 for $6,600 cash (ii) paid an extra $2,000 of capital into the business bank account (iii) bought inventory on credit for $500 (iv) withdrew $8,900 from the business bank account for personal use (v) bought office equipment for $8,500, paying by bank transfer. (a) Calculate the owner's capital at the start of the month. (b) Calculate total assets, total liabilities and capital at the end of the month.
items.answer: (a) $25,000 (b) Assets $31,000; liabilities $12,000; capital $19,000

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why drawings are debited to a drawings account rather than to the capital account directly. (b) Explain the principle of double entry.
items.answer: (a) A separate drawings account collects all withdrawals during the year so their total is visible; it is transferred to capital at the year end, keeping the capital account uncluttered. (b) Every transaction has two aspects of equal value; one account is debited and another is credited with the same amount, so total debits always equal total credits.
items.markingKey: (a) Collects withdrawals in one place/shows total [1]; transferred to capital at year end [1] [2] (b) Two aspects/dual effect [1]; equal debit and credit entries [1] [2]

items.stem: The following transactions took place at Kilimanjaro Coffee during March: (i) paid Sofia $3,450 by cheque (ii) bought goods for resale on credit from Sofia, $3,700 (iii) bought a delivery van for $6,600 on credit from Summit Motors. A trainee accountant recorded transaction (i) by debiting Bank and crediting Sofia. Explain the error and calculate the correct double entry, showing your working.
items.answer: The entries were reversed (complete reversal); liability decreases – debit; bank decreases – credit. Correct double entry: debit Sofia, credit Bank.
items.markingKey: Error explained: the entries were reversed (complete reversal); liability decreases – debit; bank decreases – credit [1]; working: correct accounts named on each side [1]; correct double entry: debit Sofia, credit Bank [1] [3]

items.stem: Ana owns Kilimanjaro Coffee. In one week the business paid Sipho $5,250 by cheque and returned goods costing $350 to Sipho. For each transaction, state the account to be debited and the account to be credited.
items.answer: (i) Dr Sipho, Cr Bank; (ii) Dr Sipho, Cr Purchases returns
items.markingKey: (i) Dr Sipho, Cr Bank [1]; (ii) Dr Sipho, Cr Purchases returns [1] [2]

items.stem: Freya owns Monsoon Garments. In one week the business bought goods for resale on credit from Samuel, $6,000; received a cheque for $4,400 from Jonas; the owner paid $5,000 of personal savings into the business bank account and the owner took goods costing $4,400 for personal use. (a) For each transaction, state the account to be debited and the account to be credited. (b) Explain why a trial balance that agrees does not prove that every transaction has been posted to the correct account.
items.answer: (a) (i) Dr Purchases, Cr Samuel; (ii) Dr Bank, Cr Jonas; (iii) Dr Bank, Cr Capital; (iv) Dr Drawings, Cr Purchases (b) Errors such as commission, principle, omission and complete reversal keep debits equal to credits.
items.markingKey: (a) (i) Dr Purchases, Cr Samuel [1]; (ii) Dr Bank, Cr Jonas [1]; (iii) Dr Bank, Cr Capital [1]; (iv) Dr Drawings, Cr Purchases [1] [4] (b) Equal debits and credits still possible [1]; any named example of error not revealed [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain what a debit balance on a supplier's account would mean. (b) Explain why a business keeps a separate ledger account for each credit customer.
items.answer: (a) The business has paid the supplier more than it owes (e.g. overpayment or returns after payment), so the supplier owes the business – it is an asset. (b) So that the amount owed by each customer is known, statements can be sent and overdue debts chased.
items.markingKey: (a) Supplier owes the business/overpayment [1]; treated as an asset/receivable [1] [2] (b) Know amount owed by each customer [1]; credit control/statements [1] [2]
